title: Diffusion Maps
text:
Preface
A high dimensional biological measurement can follow a smooth path even when that path is curved and hard to see. A cell moving through a developmental process changes thousands of measured genes at once, although the process may have only one or two main directions of change. The straight line distance between two measurements can cut through regions where no observations occur and may not reflect their separation along the observed process.
Diffusion maps are a nonlinear dimensionality reduction method for this setting. The method builds a graph from local relationships and studies how a random walk moves through it. Observations are close in the resulting coordinates when random walks starting from them spread through the graph in similar ways.
Start with Understanding diffusion maps.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.1 What a diffusion map does
A diffusion map gives each observation a small set of new coordinates, usually named DC1, DC2, DC3, and so on. Observations receive similar coordinates when they are connected through many short steps in the original data.
The method is useful when the data follow a continuous shape that is hard to see in the measured variables. In a developmental process, many genes may change even when the main underlying changes are progression and a choice between branches.
A diffusion map is a dimensionality reduction method. It produces coordinates. It does not by itself:
Those analyses can use diffusion coordinates as input, but they are separate steps.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.2 Simulated example
The example contains 900 simulated observations and 30 measured variables related to a branching process. The simulation also records progression and branch membership. These two variables are used only to evaluate the results. The practice chapter includes ten additional noise variables.
Figure 1.1 shows the problem. The left panel shows the simple structure used to generate the data. The right panel shows two of the measured variables. The structure is not visible in that pair of measurements.







Figure 1.1: The simulated observations shown in the latent two dimensional space and in two measured variables.




The observations occupy a simple, curved shape inside a space with many dimensions. Such a shape is often called a manifold. Even with many measured variables, the data may have only a few main directions of change.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.3 Local and global distance
PCA describes the data using straight axes fitted across the whole dataset. That works well when the data structure is roughly flat. It is less suitable when the structure bends or branches.
A diffusion map starts with local distances instead. Nearby observations are treated as similar under the chosen distance measure. Large distances receive less direct influence.
In Figure 1.2, A and B lie on a curved path. Their straight line distance cuts across an empty part of the space. Moving along the populated path gives a better account of how they are related. Diffusion maps estimate this type of relationship by joining many reliable local comparisons.







Figure 1.2: Straight line distance compared with distance along a curved path.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.4 Step 1: build a neighborhood graph
For each observation, the method finds nearby observations and connects them in a graph. Similar neighbors receive stronger connections. Distant observations are not connected directly.
Figure 1.3 shows this graph for the simulated data. The positions in the figure use the known two dimensional structure only to make the graph easy to inspect. The graph itself was calculated from all 30 measured variables.







Figure 1.3: A neighborhood graph calculated from the 30 measured variables.




The graph changes the question from “How far apart are these two rows of the data matrix?” to “How easily can one region be reached from the other through local connections?”

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
section: 1.5 Step 2: let probability move through the graph
text:
1.5 Step 2: let probability move through the graph
The method next defines a random walk. From its current observation, the walk moves to a neighbor. A move to a more similar neighbor is more likely than a move to a less similar one.
Start the walk at one observation. After one step, only its immediate neighbors can be reached. After two steps, neighbors of those neighbors can also be reached. After eight steps, probability has spread farther along the graph.







Figure 1.4: Probability of reaching each observation after 1, 2, and 8 random walk steps from one starting point.




After 60 steps, a much larger part of the connected graph can be reached. The branch tips still have low probability because they are far from the starting point in terms of graph steps.







Figure 1.5: Probability of reaching each observation after 60 random walk steps from the same starting point.




This repeated spreading is the “diffusion” in diffusion maps. It is a calculation on the neighborhood graph, not movement observed in the original data.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
section: 1.6 Why use a random walk instead of a shortest path?
text:
1.6 Why use a random walk instead of a shortest path?
A shortest path uses only one route between two observations. A random walk uses all available routes and is therefore sensitive to how well two regions are connected.
The left side of Figure 1.6 shows two observations in a dense part of the graph. Several short routes connect their neighborhoods. The right side shows observations on opposite sides of a sparsely connected region. There are fewer routes between them.







Figure 1.6: A strongly connected pair and a pair separated by a sparse part of the graph.




The two pairs could have similar straight line distances and still behave differently in the random walk. Probability moves readily between the strongly connected neighborhoods and more slowly across the sparse connection. Diffusion maps therefore reduce the influence of a single accidental edge.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.7 Step 3: compare starting observations
Run the walk for the same number of steps from every observation. Starting at observation \(i\) produces a complete endpoint distribution, written \(P^t_{i,:}\). It contains one probability for every possible destination.

If probability starts here, where can it spread after \(t\) random walk steps, and with what probability?

“Reach” does not mean only that a destination can or cannot be reached. The full set of probabilities matters. Two starting observations are close in diffusion geometry when their endpoint distributions are similar. If walks started at two different observations spread to nearly the same destinations with nearly the same probabilities, those observations occupy similar positions in the graph’s connectivity structure.
Figure 1.7 compares these distributions after eight steps. P and a nearby observation give similar distributions. P and Q, which lie in different parts of the graph, give different distributions.







Figure 1.7: Endpoint distributions after eight steps from nearby and distant starting observations.




The numerical difference between two endpoint distributions is called diffusion distance:

small diffusion distance means the walks spread through the graph in similar ways
large diffusion distance means they spread in different ways

This comparison uses the neighborhoods and paths around both observations, not just their direct distance or a single edge. The sequence is
\[
\text{start from each observation}
\longrightarrow
\text{let probability diffuse}
\longrightarrow
\text{compare where it spreads}
\longrightarrow
\text{represent the comparisons with diffusion coordinates}.
\]

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
section: 1.8 Step 4: replace long distributions with coordinates
text:
1.8 Step 4: replace long distributions with coordinates
With \(n\) observations, every starting observation produces a profile containing \(n\) probabilities. Comparing these high dimensional profiles directly becomes cumbersome for a large dataset.
The diffusion has already occurred through the repeated random walk steps. The eigendecomposition does not create it.
The eigendecomposition provides a compact coordinate system that summarizes differences between the diffusion profiles.
A diffusion map usually returns coordinates named DC1, DC2, DC3, and so on. Using the full nontrivial eigenbasis reproduces diffusion distance exactly under this construction. Keeping only the leading components gives a lower dimensional approximation. The mathematics chapter derives this result.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
section: 1.9 The number of steps controls the scale
text:
1.9 The number of steps controls the scale
The number of random walk steps is written \(t\) and called diffusion time. Despite the name, it is not clock time, developmental time, or a measured property of the observations.

With small \(t\), the endpoint distribution covers a small neighborhood. The result retains local detail and can also retain local noise.
With intermediate \(t\), the walk covers a wider region. Small irregularities matter less, while larger structure remains.
With very large \(t\), the walk eventually loses information about where it started. Different starting observations then become hard to distinguish.

There is therefore no rule that larger \(t\) is better. The practice chapter shows how to inspect its effect. The mathematics chapter explains how \(t\) changes the relative contribution of the diffusion components.

1.9.1 When a fixed diffusion time is used
Many software packages return the diffusion eigenvectors \(\psi_k\) and eigenvalues \(\lambda_k\) without asking the user to choose \(t\). Those quantities are enough to construct coordinates at any diffusion time:
\[
\mathrm{DC}_k^{(t)} = \lambda_k^t\psi_k.
\]
Diffusion time connects the repeated walk \(P^t\) to diffusion distance. It also explains the persistence of connectivity patterns and why components with smaller eigenvalues lose influence faster.
A fixed \(t>1\) is useful when the analysis needs geometry at a chosen propagation scale. A moderate value can reduce very local differences while retaining broader structure. Because the components are reweighted by different amounts, Euclidean distances in the weighted coordinates also change. This can affect clustering, neighbor searches, and other analyses that use those distances.
Many workflows do not select a fixed \(t\). They work directly with the returned components and eigenvalues, or use a method such as Diffusion Pseudotime that draws on diffusion information across scales. A very large \(t\) is not better. On a connected graph that mixes, all nontrivial patterns eventually decay and the walk forgets its starting point.

Diffusion time is essential for understanding the method, but choosing a fixed \(t>1\) is not a mandatory step in every practical diffusion map workflow.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.10 What the diffusion components represent
Each component describes a different pattern of connectivity across the observations. Components are not original measured variables, and they are not PCA directions chosen to maximize variance.

1.10.1 Smoothness means similarity between graph neighbors
Start with a graph that is just a line of seven observations, A through G, each connected only to its immediate neighbors. Figure 1.8 (left) shows one possible component on this graph: a value assigned to each observation, changing gradually from -1 at A to 1 at G.







Figure 1.8: A smooth pattern and an alternating pattern on the same line graph.




This component describes a broad distinction between the two ends of the graph. Connected observations receive similar values, and the large difference appears only when distant parts of the graph are compared. This is what it means for a component to be smooth over the graph.
“Smooth” does not refer to chronological or biological time. It means that observations connected by strong graph edges tend to have similar component values.
A branching graph can contain more than one broad pattern. Figure 1.9 shows the simplest case: a shared trunk leading to a junction, then two separate branches.







Figure 1.9: A simple branching graph: a shared trunk from a starting observation to a junction, then two separate branches.




One component might distinguish the start from both terminal regions. Another might assign similar values along the shared trunk but opposite values to branches A and B. The same graph can therefore support components describing progression, branch separation, weakly connected regions, or smaller local features. DC1 does not always represent progression, and DC2 does not always represent branching. Their meanings depend on the graph.
Figure 1.10 illustrates three possible patterns on the simulated branching layout. These are deliberately simplified examples, not components estimated from the data. The displayed persistence values are also illustrative.







Figure 1.10: Three illustrative component patterns on the simulated branching layout.




In this illustration, DC1 with value 0.98 is the most slowly forgotten nontrivial pattern. DC2 with value 0.91 describes another persistent distinction, but it disappears faster than DC1. DC3 with value 0.45 describes a more local distinction that is erased more quickly. These numbers do not rank biological importance. A later component can still represent meaningful structure. Later does not mean noise.


1.10.2 Component order
Each random walk step mixes information between neighboring observations. Some connectivity distinctions survive this mixing for many steps. Others are removed quickly.
Consider two dense regions joined by a weak connection, shown schematically in Figure 1.11.







Figure 1.11: Two dense regions connected by a single weak edge.




A walk starting in the left region tends to remain there for several steps, and the same is true on the right. It takes many steps for the walk to forget which region it started in.
A pattern is persistent when the random walk needs many steps to forget the distinction.
Now consider the alternating pattern shown on the right side of Figure 1.8. Its value changes between 0 and 1 at every edge.
Mixing each value with its neighbors quickly flattens this alternating pattern. It is a rapidly disappearing structure.
The first nontrivial diffusion components describe distinctions that the random walk forgets most slowly. Later components describe patterns that disappear more quickly and often occur at a finer scale. This ordering is not a ranking of biological importance.


1.10.3 Component values and eigenvalues
The component values show which connectivity pattern is being described. Its eigenvalue indicates how quickly the random walk erases that pattern.
For example, a component may separate two regions joined by a weak bottleneck. Observations within each strongly connected region tend to receive similar component values, while the main change occurs across the bottleneck. If the random walk rarely crosses that bottleneck, the distinction has a large eigenvalue and remains visible for many steps.
A large diffusion eigenvalue does not mean large explained variance. Unlike a PCA eigenvalue, it is not a measure of how much variance a component explains. A value close to 1 means that one diffusion step changes the component little. A smaller value means that repeated diffusion washes out the component more quickly.
The full diffusion calculation also contains a stationary component that assigns no useful separation between observations. Software may store it internally. In Scanpy, it appears as the first stored column. Diffusion map plots normally begin with the first nontrivial component, called DC1 here. The practical chapter shows how each package stores these columns.


1.10.4 Diffusion time reweights the components
Component ordering is based on what survives one step. Diffusion time \(t\) controls how many times that step is repeated. The difference between components therefore grows with \(t\).

At small \(t\), local differences, branch differences, and broad progression may all be visible. At intermediate \(t\), many local differences have disappeared while major branches and broad progression remain. At larger \(t\), branch differences may also weaken, leaving only the broadest connectivity pattern. At extremely large \(t\), the walk eventually forgets almost all information about its starting point.
Within one component, increasing \(t\) does not change the ordering of observations. It changes the component’s scale. When several components are combined, those with smaller eigenvalues shrink faster and contribute less to multidimensional distance.
Figure 1.12 shows this on the simulated data. DC2 shrinks faster than DC1, so the map is compressed vertically as \(t\) increases. The common axis limits make that change visible.







Figure 1.12: DC1 against DC2 at three diffusion times, with fixed axis limits.




If each panel is automatically rescaled, the effect can be hidden. Figure 1.13 shows the same coordinates with separate axis limits. The shapes appear much more similar because each panel has been stretched to fill the plotting area.







Figure 1.13: The same diffusion coordinates with each panel rescaled independently.




Use fixed axis limits when comparing the relative scale of components across diffusion times.
The large values of \(t\) in these two figures were chosen to make the scaling visible. They are not recommended default settings.


1.10.5 Questions to ask about a component
When interpreting DC1, DC2, or a later component, ask:

What broad connectivity pattern does it distinguish?
Do graph neighbors have similar component values?
Does it follow progression, separate branches, cross a bottleneck, or describe a smaller local feature?
How large is its eigenvalue relative to those of the following components?
Does the pattern remain visible as diffusion time increases?
Could it reflect batch, sampling density, or another technical factor rather than the process of interest?

The component values describe the pattern. The eigenvalue describes how quickly the random walk forgets it. Component order places the most slowly forgotten nontrivial patterns first.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.11 Results for the simulated data
Figure 1.14 shows the first two components calculated from the 30 measured variables. DC1 closely follows known progression, while DC2 helps separate the two known branches. The method was not given progression or branch labels.







Figure 1.14: The first two diffusion components, colored by known progression and branch identity.




DC1’s eigenvalue is 0.9996. This says that a single diffusion step retains 99.96% of the component’s scale. It does not say that DC1 explains 99.96% of the data. In this graph, the most persistent nontrivial connectivity pattern happens to follow progression. That interpretation must be checked rather than assumed.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
section: 1.12 Coordinates are not a directed trajectory
text:
1.12 Coordinates are not a directed trajectory
The example has a strong relationship between DC1 and known progression, but the diffusion map does not know which end is early or late. Reversing the sign of DC1 would describe the same geometry.
A directed trajectory requires extra information, such as a chosen starting observation, known time labels, biological knowledge, or an independent directional measurement. Trajectory inference is a downstream analysis that can be performed on diffusion coordinates.
The same caution applies to branches. Separation in a diffusion map shows separation in the neighborhood graph. It does not establish that the groups are distinct biological fates. Batch effects, measurement artifacts, or graph settings can also produce separation.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.13 When the method is useful
Diffusion maps are a reasonable choice when:

the data appear to contain a gradual process rather than only separate groups
the structure may be curved or branching
distances between close observations are meaningful
the measured space has many dimensions but is thought to contain a structure with fewer dimensions

They are less suitable when:

no meaningful distance can be defined between observations
batch effects or other technical differences dominate the neighborhoods
nearest neighbors are unstable because the data are too sparse or noisy
the main goal is a linear model with directly interpretable feature loadings
the task is supervised prediction rather than geometric representation

A diffusion map follows the graph it is given. It cannot decide whether that graph reflects biology, a technical artifact, or poor parameter choices. Neighborhood stability and known covariates should be checked before interpreting the coordinates.

title: 1  Understanding diffusion maps
text:
1.14 Summary







Figure 1.15: The diffusion map pipeline, from observations to diffusion components.




The method can be summarized in four steps:

Connect similar observations in a neighborhood graph.
Run a random walk for \(t\) steps from each observation.
Compare the resulting endpoint distributions using diffusion distance.
Represent those comparisons with a small number of diffusion components.

The next chapter implements these steps in R and Python. The mathematics chapter then derives the transition probabilities, diffusion distance, and diffusion components.

title: 2  Diffusion maps in R and Python
text:
2.5 Using a fixed diffusion time
destiny and Scanpy return eigenvectors and eigenvalues without requiring a fixed diffusion time. They can be used to construct coordinates at any \(t\):
\[\mathrm{DC}_k^{(t)} = \lambda_k^t\psi_k.\]
Diffusion time explains \(P^t\), diffusion distance, the persistence of graph patterns, and the faster decay of components with smaller eigenvalues. It does not need to be tuned in every analysis.
A fixed \(t>1\) is most relevant when the analysis needs diffusion geometry at a particular propagation scale. Changing \(t\) changes Euclidean distances in the weighted coordinates because each component receives a different weight. Those distances may then be used for clustering, neighbor calculations, or another geometric analysis.
The example below uses \(t=1\), \(t=5\), and \(t=20\). It reports the ranges of DC1 and DC2 and the distance between an early observation and a terminal observation. The distance uses the first nine nonstationary components.

RPython


evals_r <- eigenvalues(dm)
psi_r <- dc_r[, 1:9]
pair_r <- c(
  which.min(df$true_pseudotime),
  which.max(df$true_pseudotime)
)

for (t in c(1, 5, 20)) {
  coords_t <- sweep(
    psi_r,
    2,
    evals_r[1:9]^t,
    "*"
  )
  span <- apply(coords_t[, 1:2], 2, function(v) diff(range(v)))
  pair_distance <- sqrt(sum(
    (coords_t[pair_r[1], ] - coords_t[pair_r[2], ])^2
  ))
  cat(sprintf(
    "t=%2d  DC1 range=%.4f  DC2 range=%.4f  pair distance=%.4f\n",
    t, span[1], span[2], pair_distance
  ))
}

t= 5  DC1 range=0.0929  DC2 range=0.1371  pair distance=0.1563
t=20  DC1 range=0.0905  DC2 range=0.1282  pair distance=0.1013


evals_py = adata.uns["diffmap_evals"]
psi_py = adata.obsm["X_diffmap"][:, 1:10]
pair_py = [
    int(df["true_pseudotime"].idxmin()),
    int(df["true_pseudotime"].idxmax()),
]

for t in (1, 5, 20):
    coords_t = psi_py * (evals_py[1:10] ** t)[None, :]
    span = coords_t[:, :2].max(axis=0) - coords_t[:, :2].min(axis=0)
    pair_distance = np.linalg.norm(
        coords_t[pair_py[0]] - coords_t[pair_py[1]]
    )
    print(
        f"t={t:2d}  DC1 range={span[0]:.4f}  "
        f"DC2 range={span[1]:.4f}  "
        f"pair distance={pair_distance:.4f}"
    )
t= 1  DC1 range=0.0975  DC2 range=0.1385  pair distance=0.1972
t= 5  DC1 range=0.0968  DC2 range=0.1365  pair distance=0.1671
t=20  DC1 range=0.0945  DC2 range=0.1290  pair distance=0.1122



The first two eigenvalues are close to 1, so the ranges of DC1 and DC2 change moderately. The pairwise distance changes more because it includes later components with smaller eigenvalues. Those components lose weight faster as \(t\) increases.







Figure 2.4: The first two weighted diffusion coordinates at three values of diffusion time, shown with fixed axis limits.




Fixed axis limits are necessary for this comparison. If each panel rescales its axes independently, the plots can look unchanged even when the pairwise distances have decreased.
Many workflows use the returned eigenvectors and eigenvalues directly or use methods such as Diffusion Pseudotime that combine diffusion information across scales. They do not require the analyst to select one fixed \(t\). Very large values are not better because every nonstationary component eventually decays on a connected graph that mixes.

Diffusion time is essential for understanding the method, but choosing a fixed \(t>1\) is not a mandatory step in every practical diffusion map workflow.

2.6.1 Number of neighbors
The neighbor count controls how many local connections are available to each observation.

for (k_try in c(4, 15, 120)) {
  set.seed(1)
  dm_k <- DiffusionMap(X, k = k_try, n_eigs = 5)

  cat(sprintf(
    "k=%4d  |corr|=%.3f  eigenvalues=%.4f, %.4f\n",
    k_try,
    abs(c1),
    eigenvalues(dm_k)[1],
    eigenvalues(dm_k)[2]
  ))
}

n_neighbors= 120  |corr|=0.683  eigenvalues=[1.     0.9907]

With 4 neighbors, Scanpy produces a fragmented embedding and destiny remains connected enough to retain the main progression. With 120 neighbors, both methods connect observations across wider regions and the correlation with progression decreases. The same neighbor count does not produce an identical graph in the two packages.


2.6.2 Kernel settings
The packages expose different kernel controls. In destiny, sigma controls the bandwidth. In Scanpy, method selects the connectivity construction. These settings are related but are not direct equivalents.

RPython


sig <- find_sigmas(X, verbose = FALSE)
sigma_auto <- optimal_sigma(sig)

for (sigma_try in c(1, sigma_auto, 100)) {
  set.seed(1)
  dm_s <- DiffusionMap(
    X,
    k = 15,
    sigma = sigma_try,
    n_eigs = 5
  )
  c1 <- cor(eigenvectors(dm_s)[, 1], df$true_pseudotime)
  cat(sprintf(
    "sigma=%7.3f  |corr|=%.3f\n",
    sigma_try,
    abs(c1)
  ))
}

sigma=  2.934  |corr|=0.928
sigma=100.000  |corr|=0.919

    a = ad.AnnData(X=X.astype("float32"))

        a,
        n_neighbors=15,
        method=method,
        use_rep="X"
    )
    sc.tl.diffmap(a, n_comps=5)
    c1 = np.corrcoef(
        a.obsm["X_diffmap"][:, 1],
        df["true_pseudotime"]
    )[0, 1]
    print(f"method={method:6s}  |corr|={abs(c1):.3f}")

method=gauss   |corr|=0.919



A narrow bandwidth in destiny weakens communication beyond the closest observations and reduces the progression correlation. The broad bandwidth has a smaller effect because the neighbor count still limits which pairs can be connected. Scanpy’s two kernel methods give similar results on this dataset.







Figure 2.6: Scanpy diffusion embeddings using the UMAP and Gaussian connectivity methods.




destiny also provides density_norm. Scanpy does not expose an equivalent switch, so the settings are not directly comparable. Density normalization is derived in Chapter 3.

Both packages return more components when requested. The first nine are compared with known progression and with one of the simulated noise variables.

2.7 Diffusion pseudotime
Diffusion coordinates describe geometry without assigning a direction. Diffusion Pseudotime uses a selected root observation to orient that geometry.
The root below is the observation with the smallest known simulation time. With observed data, the root must be supported by experimental information or subject knowledge.

root_r <- which.min(df$true_pseudotime)
dpt_r <- DPT(dm, tips = root_r)

round(cor(dpt_r$DPT1, df$true_pseudotime), 3)
[1] 0.96


root_py = int(df["true_pseudotime"].idxmin())
adata.uns["iroot"] = root_py

    adata.obs["dpt_pseudotime"],
    df["true_pseudotime"]

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.1 From distances to transition probabilities
A diffusion map starts with pairwise distances and ends with coordinates that represent diffusion distance. The full coordinate set gives the distance exactly, while a truncated set gives an approximation. The construction has four parts:
The same five observations are used throughout the derivation:
\[x = (0, 1, 2, 4, 5).\]
Observations 1, 2, and 3 form one close group. Observations 4 and 5 form another. The gap between observations 3 and 4 is 2, while the other adjacent gaps are 1. This uneven spacing provides a small example of two regions connected more weakly than observations within either region.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.1.1 Pairwise distance
Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) be observations in \(p\) dimensions. Their Euclidean distances are
\[r_{ij} = \lVert x_i - x_j \rVert.\]
Here \(n=5\) and \(p=1\), so \(r_{ij}=|x_i-x_j|\). The distance matrix is
\[r =
\begin{pmatrix}
0 & 1 & 2 & 4 & 5 \\
1 & 0 & 1 & 3 & 4 \\
2 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 3 \\
4 & 3 & 2 & 0 & 1 \\
5 & 4 & 3 & 1 & 0
\end{pmatrix}.\]
The construction treats short distances as reliable local comparisons. Long distances are not discarded because they are numerically wrong. They are given little direct influence because they do not describe how the observations between the two endpoints are connected.


3.1.2 Similarity kernel
A Gaussian kernel converts distance into similarity:
\[K_{ij} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{r_{ij}^2}{\epsilon}\right).\]
The bandwidth \(\epsilon\) controls how quickly similarity decreases. The numerical example uses \(\epsilon=2\). A distance of 0 gives similarity 1, a distance of 1 gives \(\exp(-1/2)=0.607\), and a distance of 5 gives about \(4\times10^{-6}\).
The kernel matrix is
\[K =
\begin{pmatrix}
1      & 0.6065 & 0.1353 & 0.0003 & 0.0000 \\
0.6065 & 1      & 0.6065 & 0.0111 & 0.0003 \\
0.1353 & 0.6065 & 1      & 0.1353 & 0.0111 \\
0.0003 & 0.0111 & 0.1353 & 1      & 0.6065 \\
0.0000 & 0.0003 & 0.0111 & 0.6065 & 1
\end{pmatrix}.\]
The direct similarities \(K_{13}\) and \(K_{34}\) are both 0.1353 because both pairs are separated by distance 2. The kernel alone does not distinguish a pair inside the first group from a pair that crosses the larger gap. That distinction will come from their connections to the other observations.
Some software writes the denominator as \(2\sigma^2\) instead of \(\epsilon\). These are two parameterizations of the same kernel.


3.1.3 Local graph
Large datasets normally retain only the \(k\) nearest neighbors of each observation. The graph is then symmetrized so that the retained connections can be treated consistently in both directions.
The neighbor count and the bandwidth have different roles:

\(k\) determines which edges exist.
\(\epsilon\) determines the weight of an existing edge.

The five observation example keeps the full kernel because every entry can be displayed. Chapter 2 uses sparse neighbor graphs for the larger simulated dataset.


3.1.4 Sampling density
The row sum of the kernel is
\[q_i = \sum_j K_{ij}.\]
For the example,
\[q = (1.742, 2.224, 1.888, 1.753, 1.618).\]
\(q_i\) measures how much kernel similarity surrounds observation \(i\). Observation 2 has the largest value because it lies close to observations 1 and 3. Observation 5 has the smallest value because it has only one close neighbor.
These row sums reflect both the shape of the data and how densely that shape was sampled. A densely sampled region can receive stronger total connectivity even when density is not the feature the analysis is intended to preserve.


3.1.5 Density normalization
Density normalization adjusts the kernel before it is turned into transition probabilities:
\[K_{ij}^{(\alpha)} =
\frac{K_{ij}}{q_i^\alpha q_j^\alpha}.\]
The parameter \(\alpha\) controls how much the original sampling density affects the final graph:

\(\alpha=0\) leaves the kernel unchanged.
\(\alpha=1\) applies the strongest correction among these common choices.
\(\alpha=1/2\) gives an intermediate correction.

No value is appropriate for every application. If density differences are technical, reducing their influence can help. If density is scientifically meaningful, a strong correction can remove relevant structure.
Using \(\alpha=1/2\) gives
\[K^{(1/2)} =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.574 & 0.308 & 0.075 & 0.000 & 0.000 \\
0.308 & 0.450 & 0.296 & 0.006 & 0.000 \\
0.075 & 0.296 & 0.530 & 0.074 & 0.006 \\
0.000 & 0.006 & 0.074 & 0.570 & 0.360 \\
0.000 & 0.000 & 0.006 & 0.360 & 0.618
\end{pmatrix}.\]
Density normalization changes what the edge weights represent. A separate row normalization is still needed to turn those weights into probabilities.


3.1.6 Transition matrix
Let
\[d_i = \sum_j K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}.\]
Divide each row by its sum:
\[P_{ij} = \frac{K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}}{d_i}.\]
Every row now sums to 1:
\[\sum_j P_{ij}
= \frac{\sum_j K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}}{d_i}
= 1.\]
\(P_{ij}\) is the probability of moving from observation \(i\) to observation \(j\) in one step. The matrix \(P\) is the transition matrix:
\[P =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.600 & 0.322 & 0.078 & 0.000 & 0.000 \\
0.291 & 0.424 & 0.279 & 0.005 & 0.000 \\
0.076 & 0.302 & 0.540 & 0.076 & 0.007 \\
0.000 & 0.006 & 0.074 & 0.564 & 0.356 \\
0.000 & 0.000 & 0.007 & 0.366 & 0.628
\end{pmatrix}.\]
Row 3 shows the possible moves from observation 3. The walk remains at observation 3 with probability 0.540, moves to observation 2 with probability 0.302, and moves across the larger gap to observation 4 with probability 0.076.
\(P\) can also act on a vector of values \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_n)^\top\) assigned to the observations:
\[(Pf)_i = \sum_j P_{ij}f_j.\]
Because the weights in row \(i\) sum to 1, \((Pf)_i\) is a weighted average of the values available from observation \(i\). This neighbor averaging interpretation will be used when eigenvectors are introduced.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.2 Walking for several steps

3.2.1 Two steps
To move from \(i\) to \(j\) in two steps, the walk must pass through an intermediate observation \(k\). The probability of the route \(i\to k\to j\) is
\[P_{ik}P_{kj}.\]
Summing over every possible intermediate observation gives
\[\sum_k P_{ik}P_{kj} = (P^2)_{ij}.\]
For the route from observation 1 to observation 5,
\[(P^2)_{1,5}
= \sum_k P_{1k}P_{k5}
= 0.000633.\]
The one step probability \(P_{1,5}\) rounds to zero in the displayed matrix. Two steps allow routes through intermediate observations and therefore give a larger probability.


3.2.2 From two steps to \(t\) steps
The same multiplication gives three steps, four steps, and any later number of steps:
\[(P^t)_{ij}
= \Pr(X_t=j\mid X_0=i).\]
This entry sums the probabilities of every route of length \(t\) from \(i\) to \(j\). It is not a shortest path calculation. Routes that pass through many well connected alternatives contribute more total probability than an isolated route.


3.2.3 Where diffusion enters the construction
Constructing \(P\) defines only one random walk step. The diffusion process is the repeated propagation of probability through
\[P,\quad P^2,\quad P^3,\quad\ldots,\quad P^t,\]
where \((P^t)_{ij}\) is the probability of reaching observation \(j\) after starting at observation \(i\) and taking \(t\) steps. The conceptual sequence is
\[\text{local similarity}
\longrightarrow
\text{one step transition matrix}
\longrightarrow
\text{repeated propagation through }P^t
\longrightarrow
\text{diffusion distance}
\longrightarrow
\text{diffusion coordinates}.\]
The eigendecomposition is not the diffusion. It represents repeated diffusion efficiently because
\[P^t\psi_k=\lambda_k^t\psi_k.\]
Plotting unweighted eigenvectors of \(P\) gives a spectral embedding of the graph. A diffusion map additionally defines similarity through the \(t\) step endpoint distributions and uses the coordinates
\[\left(
\lambda_1^t\psi_1(i),
\lambda_2^t\psi_2(i),
\ldots
\right)\]
to represent the corresponding diffusion distance.
Diffusion occurs through repeated random walk propagation. The eigenvectors and eigenvalues provide a compact coordinate system for the resulting diffusion geometry.


3.2.4 Endpoint distributions
For a fixed starting observation \(i\), the row \(P^t_{i,:}\) is the distribution of possible endpoints after \(t\) steps. The one step and five step matrices are
\[P^1 =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.600 & 0.322 & 0.078 & 0.000 & 0.000 \\
0.291 & 0.424 & 0.279 & 0.005 & 0.000 \\
0.076 & 0.302 & 0.540 & 0.076 & 0.007 \\
0.000 & 0.006 & 0.074 & 0.564 & 0.356 \\
0.000 & 0.000 & 0.007 & 0.366 & 0.628
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
P^5 =
\begin{pmatrix}
0.333 & 0.338 & 0.265 & 0.044 & 0.021 \\
0.306 & 0.326 & 0.271 & 0.061 & 0.036 \\
0.258 & 0.293 & 0.263 & 0.104 & 0.081 \\
0.042 & 0.064 & 0.101 & 0.387 & 0.406 \\
0.020 & 0.039 & 0.081 & 0.417 & 0.444
\end{pmatrix}.\]
At \(t=1\), the rows remain strongly concentrated near their starting observations. At \(t=5\), rows 1, 2, and 3 have become more similar to one another. Rows 4 and 5 have also become more similar. The difference between the two groups remains because probability crosses the gap less readily than it moves within either group.
Increasing diffusion time removes distinctions within strongly connected regions before it removes distinctions between weakly connected regions.


3.2.5 Diffusion time
The number of steps \(t\) is called diffusion time. It is a count of graph transitions, not elapsed experimental or biological time.
Small values of \(t\) retain local detail. Moderate values allow local differences to mix while broader connectivity patterns remain. Very large values eventually remove all information about the starting observation when the graph is connected and mixing.
The value of \(t\) appears in both \(P^t\) and diffusion distance. Choosing one fixed \(t>1\) is not required by every software workflow. Packages often return eigenvectors and eigenvalues, which are enough to construct coordinates for any \(t\). A fixed value is most useful when an analysis needs geometry at a selected propagation scale.


3.2.6 Stationary distribution
A probability distribution over the observations is written as a row vector \(\mu^\top\). After one step it becomes
\[\mu^\top P,\]
and after \(t\) steps it becomes
\[\mu^\top P^t.\]
Starting at one observation is a special case. If \(e_i^\top\) places all probability on observation \(i\), then
\[e_i^\top P^t = P^t_{i,:}.\]
This is why the rows of \(P^t\) are endpoint distributions.
A stationary distribution is a probability distribution that does not change after another step. It is written \(\pi^\top\) and satisfies
\[\pi^\top P = \pi^\top.\]
For the graph construction used here, let
\[Z=\sum_j d_j.\]
The stationary probability of observation \(i\) is
\[\pi_i = \frac{d_i}{Z}.\]
The reason is the symmetry of \(K^{(\alpha)}\). Since
\[\begin{aligned}
d_iP_{ij} &= K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}, \\
d_jP_{ji} &= K_{ji}^{(\alpha)},
\end{aligned}\]
symmetry gives
\[\pi_iP_{ij}
= \frac{K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}}{Z}
= \frac{K_{ji}^{(\alpha)}}{Z}
= \pi_jP_{ji}.\]
This equality is called detailed balance. At stationarity, the probability flow from \(i\) to \(j\) is balanced by the flow from \(j\) to \(i\). Summing over \(i\) gives
\[\sum_i \pi_iP_{ij}=\pi_j,\]
which is the stationary equation \(\pi^\top P=\pi^\top\).
For the five observation example,
\[\pi = (0.192, 0.212, 0.196, 0.202, 0.197).\]
These values are close to uniform because the five row sums \(d_i\) are similar. On a graph with more uneven connectivity, the stationary distribution places more mass in regions with larger \(d_i\).
When the graph is connected and the walk is mixing, every initial distribution approaches \(\pi\). In this example, every row of \(P^{200}\) agrees with \(\pi\) to four decimal places. After that many steps, the endpoint distribution no longer records where the walk began.
The transition matrix will now appear in two forms. The distinction explains why the stationary distribution is a left eigenvector while diffusion components are right eigenvectors.








Object acted on by \(P\)
Operation
Interpretation




Probability row \(\mu^\top\)
\(\mu^\top P\)
Move probability forward by one step


Value pattern \(f\)
\(Pf\)
Average future values over the possible next steps



The stationary distribution satisfies \(\pi^\top P=\pi^\top\), so it is a left eigenvector with eigenvalue 1. A right eigenvector satisfies \(P\psi=\lambda\psi\) and describes a value pattern over the observations. Reversibility, expressed by detailed balance, connects these two views.
The stationary distribution is not a separate side calculation. It has two roles below. It gives the long run baseline used to compare endpoint probabilities, and it supplies the weights under which the right eigenvectors become orthogonal.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.3 Diffusion distance
Two starting observations are similar in diffusion geometry when their endpoint distributions are similar. An unweighted comparison would be
\[\sum_k \left(P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}\right)^2.\]
This gives the same weight to every destination. Destinations with large stationary probability are visited often from many starting points, so a difference there carries less information about the start. Diffusion distance accounts for this baseline frequency by dividing the squared difference at destination \(k\) by \(\pi_k\):
\[\boxed{
D_t^2(i,j)
= \sum_k
\frac{\left(P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}\right)^2}{\pi_k}.
}\]
The same absolute difference therefore counts less at a common destination with large \(\pi_k\) and more at a less common destination with small \(\pi_k\). This adjustment matters most when the stationary distribution is uneven. In this example, \(\pi\) is nearly uniform, so the weighting is close to a common rescaling.
At \(t=1\),
\[D_1(1,3)=1.596,
\qquad
D_1(3,4)=1.830,
\qquad
D_1(1,5)=2.247.\]
The raw distances \(r_{13}\) and \(r_{34}\) are both 2. Their diffusion distances differ. Observations 1 and 3 lie within the same well connected region, while observations 3 and 4 lie on opposite sides of the weaker connection. Diffusion distance includes the surrounding routes, not only the direct distance between the pair.
\(D_t\) depends on diffusion time. Changing \(t\) changes the endpoint distributions and therefore changes the geometry being measured.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
section: 3.4 Components as patterns on the graph
text:
3.4 Components as patterns on the graph

3.4.1 Why right eigenvectors appear
The rows of \(P^t\) describe how probability moves from each starting observation. Comparing those rows directly requires \(n\) values for every start. The aim is to summarize their main differences with fewer numbers.
To do this, consider a column vector \(f\) that assigns one value to every observation. The \(i\)th entry of \(Pf\) is
\[(Pf)_i
= \sum_j P_{ij}f(j).\]
This is the expected value of \(f\) after one step when the walk starts at observation \(i\):
\[(Pf)_i
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[f(X_1)\mid X_0=i\right].\]
Probability distributions move from the left as \(\mu^\top P\). Value patterns are evaluated from the right as \(Pf\). Diffusion components use the second operation because a component assigns a value to each observation.
Now suppose that the value pattern is a right eigenvector \(\psi_\ell\):
\[P\psi_\ell = \lambda_\ell\psi_\ell.\]
For every starting observation \(i\), this means
\[(P\psi_\ell)_i
= \mathbb{E}\!\left[\psi_\ell(X_1)\mid X_0=i\right]
= \lambda_\ell\psi_\ell(i).\]
The neighbor average has the same pattern as \(\psi_\ell\), multiplied by \(\lambda_\ell\). If \(\lambda_\ell\) is close to 1, one transition changes the pattern little. Strongly connected observations therefore tend to have similar component values.
A pattern that alternates sharply between neighboring observations is changed substantially by averaging. It receives a smaller eigenvalue and loses influence more quickly under repeated diffusion.
A right eigenvector is therefore useful for two related reasons. It assigns one coordinate value to each observation, and its evolution through repeated random walk steps is easy to calculate. A diffusion eigenvalue is not explained variance. It measures how strongly the corresponding graph pattern survives one transition step.


3.4.2 Repeated averaging
Applying \(P\) twice gives
\[P^2\psi_\ell
= P(P\psi_\ell)
= P(\lambda_\ell\psi_\ell)
= \lambda_\ell^2\psi_\ell.\]
After \(t\) steps,
\[\boxed{
P^t\psi_\ell = \lambda_\ell^t\psi_\ell.
}\]
For a walk starting at observation \(i\),
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\psi_\ell(X_t)\mid X_0=i\right]
= \lambda_\ell^t\psi_\ell(i).\]
The starting value \(\psi_\ell(i)\) tells us where observation \(i\) lies on the pattern. The factor \(\lambda_\ell^t\) tells us how much of that pattern remains after \(t\) steps.
Consider three illustrative eigenvalues:
\[\lambda_1=0.98,
\qquad
\lambda_2=0.80,
\qquad
\lambda_3=0.25.\]
Their powers are
\[\begin{array}{c|ccc}
t & \lambda_1^t & \lambda_2^t & \lambda_3^t \\ \hline
1  & 0.980 & 0.800 & 0.250 \\
5  & 0.904 & 0.328 & 0.001 \\
20 & 0.668 & 0.012 & 0.000 \\
50 & 0.364 & 0.00001 & 0.000
\end{array}\]
The first pattern remains visible over many steps. The third is nearly absent by \(t=5\). This persistence determines the usual ordering of diffusion components. The first nontrivial components correspond to patterns that repeated diffusion removes most slowly. Later components can still represent meaningful structure, but they disappear faster.


3.4.3 Constant component
Every row of \(P\) sums to 1, so
\[P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}.\]
The constant vector is therefore a right eigenvector with eigenvalue 1:
\[\lambda_0=1,
\qquad
\psi_0=\mathbf{1}.\]
It assigns the same value to every observation and cannot separate them. Diffusion embeddings omit this component.
The constant right eigenvector and the stationary distribution have different roles. \(\mathbf{1}\) is unchanged when \(P\) acts on a pattern from the right. \(\pi^\top\) is unchanged when a probability distribution acts on \(P\) from the left:
\[P\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1},
\qquad
\pi^\top P=\pi^\top.\]
Some software stores the constant component as column 0. The practical chapter shows this behavior in Scanpy.
If the graph has several disconnected pieces, eigenvalue 1 occurs once for each piece. Several eigenvalues extremely close to 1 can indicate regions that communicate only weakly.


3.4.4 Symmetric form used for computation
\(P\) is generally not symmetric, so its right eigenvectors need not be orthogonal under the ordinary Euclidean inner product. Detailed balance supplies a different inner product that matches the random walk:
\[\langle f,g\rangle_\pi
= \sum_i f(i)g(i)\pi_i.\]
Under this weighted inner product, \(P\) behaves like a symmetric operator:
\[\langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi
= \langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi.\]
To see this, expand the left side and use detailed balance:
\[\begin{aligned}
\langle f,Pg\rangle_\pi
&= \sum_{i,j} f(i)P_{ij}g(j)\pi_i \\
&= \sum_{i,j} f(i)P_{ji}g(j)\pi_j \\
&= \langle Pf,g\rangle_\pi.
\end{aligned}\]
Right eigenvectors associated with different eigenvalues can therefore be chosen to be orthogonal under \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_\pi\).
The same property can be expressed with an ordinary symmetric matrix. Define
\[D_\alpha = \operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n)\]
and the symmetric matrix
\[S
= D_\alpha^{-1/2}K^{(\alpha)}D_\alpha^{-1/2}.\]
\(S\) and \(P\) are related by
\[S = D_\alpha^{1/2}PD_\alpha^{-1/2}.\]
This is a similarity transformation, so \(S\) and \(P\) have the same eigenvalues. If \(\phi_\ell\) is an eigenvector of \(S\), then \(D_\alpha^{-1/2}\phi_\ell\) is a right eigenvector of \(P\).
An eigenvector can be multiplied by any nonzero constant. If \(\phi_\ell\) has ordinary Euclidean norm 1, the weighted normalized right eigenvector is
\[\psi_\ell
= \sqrt{Z}\,D_\alpha^{-1/2}\phi_\ell.\]
This scale gives
\[\langle\psi_\ell,\psi_m\rangle_\pi
= \sum_i \psi_\ell(i)\psi_m(i)\pi_i
= \delta_{\ell m}.\]
The symmetric form is useful because numerical eigensolvers handle symmetric matrices reliably. It also explains why weighted orthogonality, rather than ordinary orthogonality, appears in the formulas for \(P\).
The eigenvalues for the five observation example are
\[\lambda = (1, 0.937, 0.493, 0.230, 0.096).\]
The first nontrivial right eigenvector is approximately
\[\psi_1
= (-0.961,-0.862,-0.603,1.121,1.312)^\top.\]
Observations 1, 2, and 3 have negative values, while observations 4 and 5 have positive values. The main change occurs across the weaker connection between observations 3 and 4. Its eigenvalue, 0.937, indicates that this distinction persists much longer than the patterns associated with 0.230 or 0.096.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.5 From endpoint distributions to coordinates

3.5.1 Expansion of the transition matrix
The eigenvector equation tells us how \(P^t\) acts on one pattern. To recover the full transition matrix, we use all of the eigenvector patterns as a basis. Knowing how \(P^t\) acts on every basis vector determines how it acts on any value pattern and therefore determines the matrix itself.
The expansion uses three facts:

The right eigenvectors \(\psi_\ell\) form a basis of value patterns on the observations.
They are orthonormal under the stationary weights \(\pi\).
Applying \(P^t\) multiplies pattern \(\ell\) by \(\lambda_\ell^t\).

Let
\[\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_n).\]
For each right eigenvector, define the row vector
\[\chi_\ell^\top
= \psi_\ell^\top\Pi.\]
Weighted orthogonality gives
\[\chi_\ell^\top\psi_m
= \psi_\ell^\top\Pi\psi_m
= \delta_{\ell m}.\]
In matrix form, detailed balance is
\[\Pi P=P^\top\Pi.\]
It follows that
\[\begin{aligned}
\chi_\ell^\top P
&= \psi_\ell^\top\Pi P \\
&= \psi_\ell^\top P^\top\Pi \\
&= (P\psi_\ell)^\top\Pi \\
&= \lambda_\ell\psi_\ell^\top\Pi \\
&= \lambda_\ell\chi_\ell^\top.
\end{aligned}\]
Thus \(\chi_\ell^\top\) is the left eigenvector paired with \(\psi_\ell\).
Before expanding \(P^t\), consider any value pattern \(f\). Since the right eigenvectors form a basis, \(f\) can be reconstructed from its coefficients in that basis:
\[f
= \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\psi_\ell
\left(\chi_\ell^\top f\right).\]
The number \(\chi_\ell^\top f\) is the coefficient of pattern \(\psi_\ell\) in \(f\). Applying \(P^t\) multiplies that coefficient by \(\lambda_\ell^t\):
\[P^t f
= \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\psi_\ell
\left(\chi_\ell^\top f\right).\]
This equality holds for every \(f\), so the matrix itself is
\[P^t
= \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\psi_\ell\chi_\ell^\top.\]
Substituting \(\chi_\ell^\top=\psi_\ell^\top\Pi\) gives
\[P^t
= \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\psi_\ell\psi_\ell^\top\Pi.\]
Taking entry \((i,k)\) produces
\[P^t_{ik}
= \pi_k
\sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\psi_\ell(i)\psi_\ell(k).\]
The component with \(\ell=0\) has \(\lambda_0=1\) and \(\psi_0=\mathbf{1}\). Its contribution is \(\pi_k\). Separating it from the sum gives
\[\boxed{
P^t_{ik}
= \pi_k
\left[
1 + \sum_{\ell\ge1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\psi_\ell(i)\psi_\ell(k)
\right].
}\]
This formula describes the endpoint probability as a stationary baseline plus corrections that retain information about the starting observation. Pattern \(\ell\) contributes through three factors:

\(\psi_\ell(i)\) records the position of the starting observation on the pattern
\(\psi_\ell(k)\) records the position of the destination on the same pattern
\(\lambda_\ell^t\) records how much of the pattern remains after \(t\) steps

As \(t\) increases, the nontrivial terms decay and only \(\pi_k\) remains. This matches the earlier observation that every row of \(P^t\) approaches the stationary distribution.
For example, the probability of moving from observation 1 to observation 5 in three steps can be separated into the stationary term and four nontrivial terms:
\[\begin{aligned}
P^3_{1,5}
&= 0.197237
- 0.204708
+ 0.012949
- 0.001090
+ 0.000029 \\
&= 0.004416.
\end{aligned}\]
The first number is \(\pi_5\). The remaining numbers are the contributions of modes 1 through 4. Individual mode contributions can be positive or negative because an eigenvector can place the start and destination on the same side or on opposite sides of a pattern. Their sum is the transition probability. Using all four nontrivial eigenpairs reconstructs \(P^3\) to within \(4\times10^{-15}\) of direct matrix multiplication.


3.5.2 Diffusion distance in the eigenvector basis
Subtract the expansion for starting observation \(j\) from the expansion for \(i\). The shared stationary term cancels:
\[P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}
= \pi_k
\sum_{\ell\ge1}
\lambda_\ell^t
\left[\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right]
\psi_\ell(k).\]
For shorter notation, define
\[a_\ell
= \lambda_\ell^t
\left[\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right].\]
The difference between the two endpoint probabilities is then
\[P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}
= \pi_k\sum_{\ell\ge1}a_\ell\psi_\ell(k).\]
Substitute this expression into diffusion distance:
\[\begin{aligned}
D_t^2(i,j)
&= \sum_k
\frac{\left(P^t_{ik}-P^t_{jk}\right)^2}{\pi_k} \\
&= \sum_k \pi_k
\left[
\sum_{\ell\ge1}a_\ell\psi_\ell(k)
\right]^2 \\
&= \sum_{\ell,m\ge1}
a_\ell a_m
\sum_k \pi_k\psi_\ell(k)\psi_m(k).
\end{aligned}\]
The last sum is \(\delta_{\ell m}\) because the eigenvectors are orthonormal under the stationary weights. Terms with \(\ell\ne m\) vanish, leaving
\[D_t^2(i,j)
= \sum_{\ell\ge1}a_\ell^2.\]
Replacing \(a_\ell\) with its definition gives
\[\boxed{
D_t^2(i,j)
= \sum_{\ell\ge1}
\lambda_\ell^{2t}
\left[\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right]^2.
}\]
The difference \(\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\) measures how far apart the observations are on pattern \(\ell\). The factor \(\lambda_\ell^{2t}\) determines how much that pattern contributes at diffusion time \(t\). The formula contains no cross terms because weighted orthogonality separates the component contributions.
For the example, this expression reproduces the distances calculated directly from the rows of \(P\) to within \(4\times10^{-15}\).


3.5.3 Diffusion coordinates
Define the diffusion map at time \(t\) by
\[\boxed{
\Phi_t(i)
= \left(
\lambda_1^t\psi_1(i),
\lambda_2^t\psi_2(i),
\ldots
\right).
}\]
The squared Euclidean distance between two coordinate vectors is
\[\begin{aligned}
\lVert\Phi_t(i)-\Phi_t(j)\rVert^2
&= \sum_{\ell\ge1}
\lambda_\ell^{2t}
\left[\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right]^2 \\
&= D_t^2(i,j).
\end{aligned}\]
Therefore
\[\boxed{
D_t(i,j)
= \lVert\Phi_t(i)-\Phi_t(j)\rVert.
}\]
With all \(n-1\) nontrivial components, this equality is exact. Keeping fewer components gives an approximation. For the five observation example, all four nontrivial coordinates reproduce the directly calculated diffusion distances to numerical precision.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
section: 3.6 Using a finite number of components
text:
3.6 Using a finite number of components

3.6.1 Truncation
Using the first \(m\) nontrivial components gives
\[\Phi_t^{(m)}(i)
= \left(
\lambda_1^t\psi_1(i),
\ldots,
\lambda_m^t\psi_m(i)
\right).\]
The omitted part of the squared diffusion distance is
\[\sum_{\ell>m}
\lambda_\ell^{2t}
\left[\psi_\ell(i)-\psi_\ell(j)\right]^2.\]
For observations 1 and 5 at \(t=1\), the full squared distance is
\[D_1^2(1,5)=5.049.\]
The first component contributes 4.538. Components 2 through 4 contribute the remaining 0.511. One component therefore preserves most of this particular distance, but not all diffusion distances need have the same concentration in DC1.
Larger \(t\) suppresses components with smaller eigenvalues more strongly. This reduces truncation error when only early components are kept, but it also removes the finer structure represented by the omitted components. Later components should not be treated as noise solely because their eigenvalues are smaller.


3.6.2 Relative weighting across components
Multiplying one component by a constant does not change the ordering of observations on that component. For example,
\[\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}
\quad\text{and}\quad
0.5
\begin{pmatrix}-2\\-1\\0\\1\\2\end{pmatrix}\]
describe the same pattern in one dimension at different scales.
Diffusion time matters when several components are used together. Each component is multiplied by a different factor \(\lambda_\ell^t\). Using
\[\lambda_1=0.98,
\qquad
\lambda_2=0.80,
\qquad
\lambda_3=0.30,\]
at \(t=5\) gives
\[\lambda_1^5=0.90392,
\qquad
\lambda_2^5=0.32768,
\qquad
\lambda_3^5=0.00243.\]
The third component then contributes very little to a multidimensional distance compared with the first. Increasing \(t\) changes the relative weighting of the axes even though it does not reorder observations within an individual axis.
Figure 3.1 shows this effect for the first three eigenvalues of the simulated dataset.







Figure 3.1: The first three diffusion eigenvalues raised to increasing powers of \(t\).




Plots can hide this change when each panel chooses its own axis limits. Figure 1.12 uses fixed limits and reveals the contraction. Figure 1.13 uses separate limits and makes the same coordinates look more similar.


3.6.3 When a fixed diffusion time is used
Many packages return \(\psi_\ell\) and \(\lambda_\ell\) rather than requiring the analyst to choose \(t\). These outputs define coordinates for any diffusion time:
\[\mathrm{DC}_\ell^{(t)}
= \lambda_\ell^t\psi_\ell.\]
A fixed \(t>1\) is useful when the downstream analysis needs a particular propagation scale. Changing \(t\) changes Euclidean distances across the weighted coordinates. It can therefore affect clustering, nearest neighbor calculations, and other geometric analyses.
Many workflows instead use the eigenvectors and eigenvalues directly or use trajectory methods that combine diffusion information across scales. Selecting a fixed \(t>1\) is not a mandatory step. At very large \(t\), every nontrivial term \(\lambda_\ell^t\) approaches zero on a connected mixing graph, and the starting observations become indistinguishable.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.7 Effects of graph construction

3.7.1 Bandwidth and neighbor count
The bandwidth and neighbor count affect different parts of the graph:

A small bandwidth makes edge weights decay quickly.
A large bandwidth gives more similar weights to near and moderately distant neighbors.
A small neighbor count can fragment the graph.
A large neighbor count can introduce shortcuts across the structure.

If the graph is disconnected, eigenvalue 1 appears more than once. If it is nearly disconnected, several eigenvalues can lie very close to 1. This is why an accumulation of near 1 eigenvalues can signal weak communication between graph regions rather than several useful biological processes.
An adaptive bandwidth uses a separate local scale for each observation. It can help when sampling density varies enough that one global bandwidth does not fit all regions. destiny uses a local bandwidth by default. Scanpy exposes different graph construction methods, as shown in Chapter 2.


3.7.2 Density normalization
The parameter \(\alpha\) acts before row normalization:
\[K_{ij}^{(\alpha)}
= \frac{K_{ij}}{q_i^\alpha q_j^\alpha}.\]
It controls how strongly local sampling density affects the final geometry. This choice cannot be made from the equations alone. It depends on whether density variation represents sampling bias, biological occupancy, or another feature of the data.

title: 3  Mathematics of diffusion maps
text:
3.8 Extensions

3.8.1 Continuous limit
The finite graph construction has a continuous counterpart. On a smooth manifold, diffusion is described by an operator of Laplace type. Under suitable assumptions about the kernel and sampling, the graph operator converges to a continuous diffusion operator as the number of observations grows.
The eigenfunctions of the continuous operator play the same role as the graph eigenvectors. Slowly decaying eigenfunctions describe broad structure, while rapidly decaying eigenfunctions describe finer variation. A proof of this convergence requires analysis beyond the finite matrix derivation used here.


3.8.2 New observations
A diffusion map can be fitted on a reference dataset and extended to new observations. The new observation is connected to the reference data with the same kernel. Its coordinates are then estimated from those similarities and the existing eigenpairs.
This procedure is called a Nyström extension. It avoids recomputing the full eigendecomposition, although implementation support differs across packages.

title: 4  Diffusion maps exercises
text:
4.3 Exercise 2. Build a diffusion map
Task. Construct a diffusion map from the 48 gene columns. Use \(k=20\) neighbors and plot the eigenvalue spectrum. Does the spectrum contain a distinct gap that suggests where to truncate the coordinates?






TipTip



The file already contains normalized qPCR measurements. The examples below do not apply additional scaling.








NoteSolution






RPython


library(destiny)

gene_cols <- setdiff(colnames(df), c("cell_id", "num_cells"))
X <- as.matrix(df[, gene_cols])

set.seed(1)
dm <- DiffusionMap(X, k = 20, n_eigs = 10)
evals <- eigenvalues(dm)
round(evals[1:8], 4)

plot(seq_along(evals), evals,
     type = "b", xlab = "Nonstationary component",
     ylab = "Eigenvalue")
   DC1    DC2    DC3    DC4    DC5    DC6    DC7    DC8
0.9915 0.9758 0.9320 0.9191 0.8874 0.8439 0.8126 0.7954


import scanpy as sc
import anndata as ad
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

X = df[gene_cols].to_numpy()
adata = ad.AnnData(X=X.astype("float32"))
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=20, use_rep="X")
sc.tl.diffmap(adata, n_comps=10)
evals = adata.uns["diffmap_evals"]
evals[1:9].round(4)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(range(1, len(evals)), evals[1:], "o-")
ax.set(xlabel="Nonstationary component", ylabel="Eigenvalue")
plt.show()
array([0.9924, 0.9816, 0.9521, 0.9401, 0.9134, 0.8916, 0.8666, 0.8514])










Figure 4.1: Eigenvalue spectrum of the Guo et al. diffusion map.




There is no sharp elbow, so the spectrum does not identify one truncation point. Several leading eigenvalues are close to one, followed by a gradual decline. The spectrum shows how quickly the modes decay, but the number of components to retain should also be checked against the structure and the downstream task.
Scanpy includes the stationary eigenvalue, \(\lambda_0=1\), as its first entry. The Python code omits that entry so that the displayed values correspond to the nonstationary components shown by destiny.

cor(dc[, 1], df$num_cells, method = "spearman")
cor(dc[, 2], df$num_cells, method = "spearman")

     pch = 16, xlab = "DC1", ylab = "DC3")

spearmanr(dc1, df["num_cells"]).correlation
spearmanr(dc2, df["num_cells"]).correlation

Figure 4.2: DC1 against DC2, and DC1 against DC3, colored by developmental stage.




DC2 tracks developmental stage more closely than DC1. Its Spearman correlation with stage has magnitude about \(0.82\), compared with about \(0.2\) for DC1. The sign differs between implementations because an eigenvector and its negative describe the same axis.
The plots also show separation among some cells from later stages along DC1. This may suggest branching, but the stage labels cannot establish what the separated groups represent. The result illustrates that DC1 is the most persistent nonstationary mode, not necessarily the coordinate most closely related to developmental progression.

4.5 Exercise 4. Relate DPT to developmental stage
Task. Run Diffusion Pseudotime with a root cell chosen from the earliest stage. Compare the resulting pseudotime with num_cells. Does pseudotime generally increase across the observed stages? What variation within a stage is hidden by the correlation coefficient?






NoteSolution






RPython


root <- which.min(df$num_cells)
dpt <- DPT(dm, tips = root)
cor(dpt$DPT1, df$num_cells, method = "spearman")

set.seed(1)
plot(jitter(log2(df$num_cells), amount = 0.12), dpt$DPT1,
     pch = 16, xlab = "Observed stage (log2 cell count)",
     ylab = "DPT pseudotime")
[1] 0.841


import scanpy as sc
import anndata as ad
import numpy as np

adata = ad.AnnData(X=X.astype("float32"))
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=20, use_rep="X")
sc.tl.diffmap(adata, n_comps=10)

root = int(df["num_cells"].idxmin())
adata.uns["iroot"] = root
sc.tl.dpt(adata, n_branchings=0)

from scipy.stats import spearmanr
spearmanr(adata.obs["dpt_pseudotime"], df["num_cells"]).correlation

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.log2(df["num_cells"].to_numpy()) + rng.normal(0, 0.12, len(df))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(x, adata.obs["dpt_pseudotime"], s=12)
ax.set(xlabel="Observed stage (log2 cell count)", ylabel="DPT pseudotime")
plt.show()
0.843










Figure 4.3: Diffusion Pseudotime plotted against observed developmental stage.




DPT pseudotime has a Spearman correlation of about 0.84 with the observed stage in both implementations. The plot adds information that this single number misses. Cells from the same stage can have different pseudotime values, and the stages with 32 and 64 cells contain two visible bands. This separation is compatible with more than one path through the expression graph, but identifying a lineage split would require independent cell type or lineage information.

text:
4.6 Exercise 5. Change the neighborhood size
Task. Rebuild the diffusion map with \(k=5\) and \(k=100\). Compare the resulting eigenvalue spectra to \(k=20\). What happens to the gap between the first few eigenvalues and the rest?






NoteSolution






RPython


spectra <- list()
for (k_try in c(5, 20, 100)) {
  dm_k <- DiffusionMap(X, k = k_try, n_eigs = 5)
  spectra[[as.character(k_try)]] <- eigenvalues(dm_k)
  cat(k_try, ":", round(spectra[[as.character(k_try)]][1:3], 4), "\n")
}

matplot(seq_along(spectra[[1]]), do.call(cbind, spectra),
        type = "b", lty = 1, xlab = "Nonstationary component",
        ylab = "Eigenvalue")
legend("bottomleft", legend = paste("k =", names(spectra)),
       col = seq_along(spectra), lty = 1, pch = seq_along(spectra))
5 : 0.996 0.9919 0.9773
20 : 0.9915 0.9758 0.932
100 : 0.9731 0.8773 0.774


spectra = {}
for k_try in (5, 20, 100):
    a = ad.AnnData(X=X.astype("float32"))
    sc.pp.neighbors(a, n_neighbors=k_try, use_rep="X")
    sc.tl.diffmap(a, n_comps=6)
    spectra[k_try] = a.uns["diffmap_evals"][1:6]
    print(k_try, spectra[k_try][:3].round(4))

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for k_try, values in spectra.items():
    ax.plot(range(1, len(values) + 1), values, "o-", label=f"k = {k_try}")
ax.set(xlabel="Nonstationary component", ylabel="Eigenvalue")
ax.legend()
plt.show()
5   [0.9971 0.9932 0.9841]
20  [0.9924 0.9816 0.9521]
100 [0.9835 0.9285 0.8591]



The leading nonstationary eigenvalues are closer to one at the smaller neighborhood size and decay more quickly at the larger neighborhood size. This indicates faster mixing as the graph becomes more densely connected. It does not by itself show that biologically meaningful structure has been lost. That conclusion would require checking the embeddings, neighborhood composition, or stability of the downstream result.
